title: Your Best Season
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of approaching life with an open and non-judgmental mind, letting go of preconceived notions and perspectives. By cultivating awareness and appreciation for the present moment, we can transform even challenging experiences into opportunities for growth and gratitude. This involves embracing impermanence and finding magic in the midst of difficulties, rather than resisting or judging them.

sentences.text: As most of you know, I've become interested in koans in the last year or so, after years of avoiding them because I couldn't figure them out.
We have a koan study group going now, which has been a nice addition to studying them alone.
It seems like it's a good idea in Zen to combine solo practice with group practice in many things.
It's great to sit alone at home by ourselves, but it's also really important and helpful to sit regularly with other people.
The same is true of studying, whether it's koans, whether it's sutras, whether it's texts like the Pali Canon or the Lojong teachings.
Group discussions help remind me that my point of view or my opinion is just my point of view.
When I'm confused or don't understand something, it's helpful to see that sometimes other people are also confused and don't understand, so I'm not alone.
It's a nice thing.
Frequently, someone else's understanding really enriches mine.
It really adds something to my understanding of what it is that we're trying to study together.
In group practice, you both give and receive, and that's a nice thing.
If you're studying by yourself, it's all on you.
The group discussions have stimulated my interest and my appreciation in the koans that we have studied.
We're not trying to figure them out.
We're just trying to see what gets stirred up in each one of us when we read these old stories and when we meditate on them.
We're working more with our hearts than our heads.
What I wanted to talk about tonight is how much I've appreciated the poems that go with the koans that we've been reading.
The koans have several parts.
There's the case, which is the question and answer between the student and the teacher.
Then there are other parts, like commentaries written by teachers who have come along later.
There's also, generally speaking, a poem written by the person who put together the koan collection.
In my earlier work with koans, I just paid no attention to the poem.
I was strictly interested in the case.
I would read the poem and just brush it off.
This time around, they really feel like an important part of the dialogue, an important part of the story being told.
I thought today I would read one case that we've studied and the poem that goes along with it, and then talk about that a little bit.
This is case 19 from the Mumen Khan, translated by Robert Aitken.
This collection of 48 koans was put together by Wu Men.
He lived in China from 1183 to 1266.
He was considered one of the leading masters of his time.
He published this collection in 1229.
It's been around a little while.
Mumen Khan means gateless gate or gateless barrier.
I'll read you the case and then I'll read you the poem, and then I'll have a few other things to say.
Here's the case.
*Jiaojiao asked Nanshuang, "What is the way?"
Nanshuang said, "Ordinary mind is the way."
Jiaojiao asked, "Should I try to direct myself towards it?"
Nanshuang said, "If you try to direct yourself, you betray your own practice."
Jiaojiao asked, "How can I know the way if I don't direct myself?"
And Nanshuang said, "The way is not subject to knowing or not knowing.
Knowing is delusion.
Not knowing is blankness.
If you truly reach the genuine way, you will find it as vast and boundless as outer space.
How can this be discussed at the level of affirmation or negation?"
And with these words, Jiaojiao had sudden realization.*
So here's Wumen's verse, or the poem that he wrote to go with this.
*Spring comes with flowers, autumn with the moon, summer with breeze, winter with snow.
When idle concerns don't hang in your mind, that is your best season.*
So I'll read that again.
*Spring comes with flowers, autumn with the moon, summer with breeze, winter with snow.
When idle concerns don't hang in your mind, that is your best season.*
To me, this poem talks about life unfolding and expressing itself all around us all the time, and trying to just experience that fully without the interference of idle concerns.
And then when this happens, we become one with the seasons.
I imagine that if each one of us defined idle concerns, there'd be kind of a long list and some differences.
But when I think of idle concerns, I think about my mind just drifting along from one thing to another with no one at the wheel.
I'm not paying much attention to what I'm doing or what I'm thinking about, and I'm not really choosing what I want to pay attention to.
When that's going on, it includes things like my preferences: I like this, I don't like that, I want this to be different.
I might be making a grocery list or having a complaint about something or making a to-do list.
Maybe I'm looking forward to something on the weekend, or maybe I'm not looking forward to something that's coming up and I'll think, oh, things will be better when this is over.
So preferences, a lot of that.
Most of these thoughts aren't useful.
They don't accomplish anything.
They don't get me anywhere.
And it really narrows my world down when I'm doing that.
I walk around a lot.
When I catch myself walking along, stewing about something, which happens fairly often, I stop and I notice I'm doing that.
I just stop and I look around.
I usually notice some things that are really beautiful, like clouds in the sky or maybe a tree and flower, something that I hadn't been paying any attention to.
When I notice those things, my world gets a lot better.
Usually the thoughts that were going through my head, again, weren't contributing anything and were maybe just negative.
I think this is what Wu Men is talking about when he says, when idle concerns don't hang in your mind, that is your best season.
Then I want to throw in another short poem.
This isn't from a koan, but it speaks to the same thing.
It's a haiku by Issa, who was a Japanese poet who lived from 1763 to 1828.
I have to credit Edie, you brought this into your class on creativity.
I just love this short little thing.
Here it is.
*Just simply alive, both of us, I and the poppy.*
I'll say that again.
*Just simply alive, both of us, I and the poppy.*

I remember a talk Norman Fischer gave up in Vancouver a few years ago, and he talked about the reason we love nature so much: nature, trees, flowers, the wind, birds, always give a hundred percent to living.
A tree doesn't complain about the weather.
It accepts whatever is happening, and it lives fully.
A poppy is just alive.
It opens to the sun.
It folds at night.
It folds when it rains.
It's just simply alive.
Can we, who are also a part of nature, move in that direction?
Reading these poems reminded me of a time a couple of years ago in the spring, and I can't remember if I told this story in one of my other talks, but I'm telling it again.
So maybe it'll be a repeat for some of you.
I was riding my bike to work one morning, and it was a cold, windy, rainy day, and I was getting pissed.
I was getting more and more angry as I was going along.
It had been a cold, wet spring, not unlike this one, and I was thinking, damn it, the weather shouldn't be like this.
It should be warmer.
I'm tired of this rain.
I was completely absorbed in my complaints.
I paid no attention to anything else, just how mad I was: jaw clenched, hands gripping the handlebars.
For some reason, I thought about this guy that I know who, about 10 years ago, had a very serious illness that left him crippled.
Prior to that, he'd been a good athlete, and while he's mentally okay now, he needs two canes to get around, or a walker, and he's bent over almost double, and he will never ride a bike again.
For some reason, I thought about him, and I realized he would be happy to be riding right now in this weather, in this rain, in the wind.
He would be delighted.
I don't know why I thought about that.
It's not someone I know very well, and the thoughts just spontaneously came up, and it just transformed it for me.
I stopped complaining, I relaxed, and of course, I noticed the weather.
It was still raining, it was still windy, it was still cold, but it was a much better ride, and I felt really grateful to have the health that allows me to just ride my bike.
That's something I hadn't even thought about.
I had just been thinking, I don't like the rain, I don't like the wind, I wish the weather was better.

I've used this lesson many times, because many times I ride in the rain or some other thing happens that I don't like, and it's been a great reminder to be grateful for the things that we have, and how adding complaints and editorials and preferences to what's happening in life usually makes things worse.
So when idle concerns don't hang in your mind, it's a better season, it's a better bike ride, it's kind of a better everything.
Another example happened more recently.
A couple of weeks ago, my wife and I went to visit my mother, my 94-year-old mother, who's in great health, and as we often do, we took a walk together through the cemetery where my father is buried.
This is a really beautiful cemetery.
There's a lot of big fir trees and native shrubs like rhododendrons and tall grass with wildflowers mixed in, and then graves here and there near a gravel path.
So it's very woodsy and very conducive to reflection.
It's very different from the manicured cemeteries that you see, mostly with all the grass cut and no trees or anything like that.
At my father's grave, I thought about the kind of person he was and how he lived his life.
He was a very good example for a lot of things, and I thought about how lucky I was to have known him for such a long time.
He was 90 when he died, so I was in my 50s.
I knew him that long, which was really lucky.
He was always kind.
He always treated people well, both strangers and friends.
He had a good sense of humor and he was very playful, and he had a lot of equanimity.
I never heard him say a mean thing about another person, which is remarkable.
Even in traffic, he wouldn't get impatient with other drivers, which to me, traffic brings out the worst in all of us.
It certainly does in me.
So I was always impressed that he could do that.
During the last few years of his life, he gradually lost all of his functioning, but he didn't complain.
He was cheerful most of the time.
So he was a great role model for a lot of things, including illness, old age, and death.
I thought about all these things while I was walking through the cemetery, and then I was looking at the different gravestones.
This is a very old cemetery, so some of the people have been there quite a long time.
You can't help but think when you're walking through a cemetery that life is limited.
Life as we know it has a beginning and an end.
It doesn't go on forever.
We all know this, but walking through a cemetery, it brings it home in a really deeply felt way.
Life has its seasons, just like nature.
We have the spring of our lives.
We have the winter of our lives.
But Wu Men's poem does not discriminate.
Any and all seasons can be your best season.
If you have no idle concerns, don't hang in your mind.
I thought that was a great reminder that just because a person's getting older and ill, that can still be your best season.
Walking through the cemetery always makes me think how we live our lives is really important.
What do you put your limited amount of life energy into?
And what kind of energy do you put in?
I also, walking through the cemetery, felt a lot of compassion for the many struggles that people go through in their lives.
I've passed grave sites where it looked like families had lost a number of young children.
There'd be the big tombstones with the long life of the mother and father, and then these little tombstones with three years, five years of life.
Imagine how hard that would be, to lose a child.
I passed one gravestone where I think the date of birth was 1855 and the death was 1939.
I thought, how would it be to live through the Civil War with all of its death and uncertainty?
And how about living through the Great Depression with years of economic hardship, and the strength that it takes to live through these kinds of events that come down on us from time to time?
So this walk actually felt a lot like formal Zen practice.
I was very aware of my surroundings, the smells, the sounds, the sights around me.
I felt grateful for all that I had received from my family and from life, and compassion for the difficulties that all of us encounter.
They're different, of course, but we all encounter them.
I was pondering all these things mentioned earlier, that life has a beginning and an end, and I didn't consider any of those idle thoughts.
But I also felt very grateful for this practice, to be able to sit regularly here with all of you and to participate in all of the activities that we have throughout the year.
It's really something, I think, what we've created here.
I really just felt the benefit of my practice come up during this walk through the cemetery.
So even though I was thinking about death and illness and all of the challenges that come up in life, it was a good experience, especially in that setting.
There was a peacefulness to it all.
It seems really valuable to me to be reminded about life's impermanence and to reflect on how we're living it.
I highly recommend occasionally taking a walk in the cemetery as a way to bring all that stuff up.
Wu Men's poem has helped me in a couple of ways.
For one thing, it's a reminder of how rich life is with nothing added.
I came across a saying that Suzuki Roshi said once, and for those of you who don't know him, he was a Japanese priest who died in 1971.
He came over from Japan in the 1950s and founded the San Francisco Zen Center and a couple of other monasteries.
Those things are still operating today, and our practice is based on those traditions.
He said, "Life is its own magic."
That's all he said.
So we don't have to add anything to it.
Life is its own magic.
Labeling all of my unnecessary mental activity as, oh, these are just idle thoughts: that's so free of judgment.
It makes it really easy to just let them go without criticizing myself or making a big deal out of it.
It's really just like returning to the breath in meditation practice.
These are just idle thoughts.
So that's what I wanted to tell you about how much this poem has added to my study of koans and how much I appreciate it.
So thank you very much.
